The largest possible statement of divine power is followed at once by a limit on what human beings may do to each other about belief. The classical discussion of what the verse forbids and whom it addresses works from a reported occasion of revelation involving families in Madinah whose sons had been brought up in another faith.

cards.hook: Europe read his geography for centuries under a wrong name
cards.caption:

In 1592 an abridged Arabic version was printed at Rome, among the first Arabic books printed in Europe with movable type. For most of two centuries European scholars cited an anonymous geographer from Nubia who had never existed.

It was a commercial venture apparently aimed at the Ottoman lands, and it failed: the typesetting was full of errors, some mangling the Arabic beyond use, which made it worthless to any Muslim buyer. For centuries every copy was thought destroyed, and a story circulated that the pope had ordered them burned.

They are pause marks, worked out so that a reciter taking a breath does not break the sense, and the system in widest use is credited to Muhammad ibn Tayfur al-Sajawandi. It is the origin of the tarawih habit of reciting a portion each night until the whole book is finished, and of mudarasa, in which two people take turns reciting to one another and correcting. What follows in practice is a division of labour that runs through Muslim ethics: the effort belongs to the person, the outcome does not. Somebody who works and does not receive has not failed at rizq, because rizq was never the thing he was doing.
